tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
13	under it.
14	
15	- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
16	- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
26	  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
27	- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
28	  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
29	  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
30	  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
31	  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
32	  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
33	- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
34	  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
35	- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
36	  eye, since the position already says it.
37	- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
38	  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
39	    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
40	    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
41	    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
42	  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
43	    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
44	    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
45	- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
46	  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
47	  the close.
48	- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
49	  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
50	  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
51	  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
52	- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
53	  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
54	  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
55	- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
56	  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
57	  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
58	  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
59	  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
60	  court until the answer comes.
61	- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
62	  Computed from the file alone.
63	- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
64	  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
65	  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
66	  thread naming the old id.
67	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
68	  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
69	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
70	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
71	- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
72	  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
73	  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
74	  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.

76	  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
77	  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
78	- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
79	  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

81	## Read Actions
82	
83	### Read messages
84	
85	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
86	
87	1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
88	   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
89	   thread is the context to read it in.
90	2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
91	
92	A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.
93	
94	### Find a thread
95	
96	Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.
97	
98	- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
99	- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
100	  its bodies.
101	- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
102	  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.
103	
104	## Write Actions
105	
106	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
107	
108	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
109	- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
110	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
111	- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
112	- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.
113	
114	Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
115	the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.
116	
117	1. Take ownership.
118	2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
119	   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
120	3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
121	   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
122	   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
123	   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
124	   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
125	   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
126	   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
127	   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).
128	
129	### Fetch
130	
131	1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
132	2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
133	   working copy, and that is a write.
134	
135	### Open a thread
136	
137	1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
138	2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
139	   file when it has one.
140	
141	### Write a line
142	
143	Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
144	author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
145	by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
146	again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
147	is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
148	the reply links the outcome by sha-link.
149	
150	1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
151	2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
152	   it has one.
153	
154	### Close a thread
155	
156	The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
157	is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
158	and the close sits in the same commit.
159	
160	1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

163	
164	- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
165	  cannot disagree with the threads.
166	- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
167	- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
168	  and a reader takes what is there.
169	- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
170	  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
171	  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
172	  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
173	  and that is the change it would take.
174	- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
175	  participants, and history is the only recourse.
176	- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
177	  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
178	  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
179	  commit the rules require.
180	- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
181	  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
182	  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

184	## Versions
185	
186	The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
187	bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
188	under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
189	rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
190	the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.
191	
192	- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
193	  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
194	  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
195	  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
196	  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
197	- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
198	  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
199	  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
200	- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
201	  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
202	  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
203	  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
204	  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
205	  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
206	  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
207	  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
208	  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
209	  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
210	- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
211	  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
212	  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
213	  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.
214	
215	## Specimen
216	
217	`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
218	and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
219	lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
220	shown after it.
221	
222	```
223	# m-41 hello
224	- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
225	- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
226	- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
227	- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
228	```
229	
230	````
231	# m-41-2 hey, and the cycle that answers it
232	
233	The cycle landed at
234	https://github.com/winksaville/def/blob/0123456789ab/TODO.md#feat-the-cycle.
235	
236	## What changed
237	
238	- one thing
239	- another, with the command that shows it:
240	
241	  ```
242	  vc-x1 validate --fast
243	  ```
244	````

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

1	# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do
2	
3	The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
4	long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
5	holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
6	place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
7	own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.
8	
9	The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
10	no hook is built.
11	
12	## What the lock is today
13	
14	- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
15	  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
16	  touches the lock.
17	- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
18	  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
19	- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
20	  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
21	  the instruction has it stop then.
22	- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.
23	
24	## What a hook could do
25	
26	A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
27	reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
28	`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
29	hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
30	leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
31	exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.
32	
33	- From the documents:
34	  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
35	  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
36	  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
37	    every call.
38	  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
39	  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
40	- From the probe:
41	  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
42	  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
43	    documents do not name that variable.
44	  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
45	  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
46	  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
47	    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
48	    as a lock should is the process id.
49	- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
50	  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
51	  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
52	- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
53	  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.
54	
55	## What two sessions do with no lock
56	
57	Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
58	with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
59	the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
60	operation log.
61	
62	- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
63	  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
64	  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
65	    commit under B's title.
66	  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
67	- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
68	  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
69	    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
70	  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
71	    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
72	  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
73	    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
74	    deleted them.
75	  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
76	    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
77	- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
78	  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
79	    same second, and every line of it parses.
80	  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
81	    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
82	- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
83	  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
84	    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
85	- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
86	  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
87	  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.
88	
89	## What was decided
90	
91	- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
92	  above.
93	- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
94	- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
95	  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
no hook is built.

## What the lock is today

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

## What was decided

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
  above.
- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
  sandbox's names into
  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.

# Closed: the last cycle's record

The last finished cycle's record, whole. A cycle's closing replaces this file's `## Closed` with
its own block from [zDOING.md](zDOING.md) and this file's references with that block's, so the
last record stays here until the next one is finished. Earlier cycles are in each landmark
commit's copy of the record.

## Closed

### docs: the session lock

(wink + agent, 2026-10-12) No Todo entry was picked for managing a session lock. The first entry
held two plans, the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run and what the session lock, `.agent-running`,
left undone, and the cycle began as a rewrite of the second. The rewrite asked for a hook that
takes the lock in the agent's place, and a day of looking into that ended in a decision not to
build one.

The session lock was added as two single-step cycles, each landing on `main`. This cycle gathers
those two with what was found today into one ladder and closes it as a trapezoid.

#### Deliberation

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`, wink's call.
  - Two sessions were tested with no lock, wink's thought, to see what the lock is worth:
    pushes minutes apart, pushes in the same second, and one session resumed in two terminals.
  - Nothing either session wrote was lost, and every transcript line parses, but the commit
    title and bodies might be missing if they happened at the same time with the first one
    committing all the work that both did.
  - One line of instruction prevents that. What was found is in
    [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), not here.
- The agent keeps taking the lock itself. Two other takers were considered, a Claude Code hook
  and `vc-x1`, and neither is built, wink's call.
  - A hook is a command Claude Code runs on its own when a session starts, so the lock would
    not depend on an agent reading the instruction and following it. A trial showed a hook can
    take the lock and hold it for as long as the session runs.
  - The hook is not built because it needs `CLAUDE_PID`, the id of the Claude Code process, to
    know when the session has ended. Claude Code's documents do not name that variable, so any
    release could drop it.
  - `vc-x1` taking the lock was thought to close a gap between the agent's probe and its hold.
    It closes none, wink's point: one asker wins a `flock`, whichever program asks.
- The current top two commits on main are being converted from being single-step
  cycles into a multi-step trapezoid, because in retrospect it should have been multi-step
  from the start, wink's call 2026-10-12.
  - Nothing published is rewritten. The two keep their ids, titles, and trailers, and the
    closing descends from both, so `main` moves forward onto it.
  - It is an exception to [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape), where a single-step cycle
    lands as it is. It covers these two commits and the versions below, and Land takes its
    own go.
- Every rung has a bare version, 0.84.25 and 0.84.26 for the two rungs made in the cycle and
  0.84.27 for the closing.
  - The first two landed bare, 0.84.23 and 0.84.24, and are published.
  - A suffixed version wants the `-dev` name beside it, and the cycle is documents alone.
- A fourth rung is inserted ahead of the closing, wink's call, 2026-10-13
  ([Unplanned work](AGENTS.md#unplanned-work)).
  - The closing's review grew Todo planning that is no bookkeeping: `TODO.md` lost the headings
    the record left behind, and two entries were reworked.
  - The closing's own edits were set aside while the rung was made, so each commit has its own
    change alone.
  - It is outside the cycle's subject and is a rung all the same, the edits being made and
    reviewed, and a cycle of its own costing an opening, a closing, and a Land.

#### Solution

The session lock stayed as it was, an instruction in `custom.md` that the agent follows.

- What a hook could do and what two sessions do without a lock are in
  [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md).
- Three Todo entries carry what is left: the proposal of the lock to the set with the
  instruction's two faults, the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run, and `init` writing the agent
  sandbox's names into `.gitignore`.
- `TODO.md` is the todo list alone, by a rung the closing's review grew.
- The lock's two landed commits and the three made in this cycle are one ladder, and the closing
  is the merge that draws the trapezoid around them at Land.

#### Acceptance check

- `vc-x1 validate` passes. Passed, on the closing.
- `custom.md` is unchanged, and no file under `src/` is changed. Failed for `custom.md` and
  passed for `src/`, compared with the trapezoid's first parent,
  `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md`.
  - `custom.md` gained the lock line, nine lines, which the first rung added and the second
    reworded.
  - Why it failed: the check was written for the work of 2026-10-12, before the first two rungs
    were counted as this cycle's, and as a trapezoid the cycle is everything since its first
    parent. The line is the cycle's subject, so the change is the intended one and the check
    was wrong.
- [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md) holds the probe's findings and the three tests, and
  each of the three Todo entries links it. Passed: the findings are under "What a hook could do",
  the tests under "What two sessions do with no lock", and the three entries, the second to
  the fourth of `## Todo`, each link the file.
- After Land, `main` is a merge of two parents, `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md`
  first and this cycle's third rung second, and `jj log -r 'main@origin..main'` prints nothing.
  Not run: Land comes after this commit, on a go of its own, and the check is made then. The
  second parent is the fourth rung, one having been inserted after the check was written.

#### Ladder

- [docs: a session takes the workspace lock at acquaint][1] (done)
- [docs: the session lock is settled as flock][2] (done)
- [docs: two sessions in one workspace, tested][3] (done)
- [docs: TODO.md is the todo list, its split completed][5] (done)
- [docs: the session lock closing][4] (done)

##### docs: a session takes the workspace lock at acquaint

Landed 2026-10-11 as a single-step cycle. A line in `custom.md` has a session probe the lock at
acquaint and hold it with a background command, or refuse in one fixed sentence.

##### docs: the session lock is settled as flock

Landed 2026-10-11 as a single-step cycle, and its record is that commit's copy of `zCLOSED.md`,
which this cycle's closing replaced. Every way a session ends releases the lock, so it is the `flock`
alone, and a resumed session takes it again.

##### docs: two sessions in one workspace, tested

The lock rested on a guess that two sessions in one workspace do harm, and on an instruction an
agent has to follow. Both were looked into, and the lock is kept as it is.

- A notes file holds what a hook could do in the agent's place and what three tests of two
  sessions with no lock showed.
- The first Todo entry, which held two plans, is two entries.
  - The session lock's is first: the proposal to the set, and the instruction's two faults.
  - The run lock's is second, with the push that died as its first evidence. Two `vc-x1` runs
    in the same second is that lock's case and not the session lock's.
- A third entry is new: `init` writes the agent sandbox's names into `.gitignore`, a test
  having committed 23 empty files the sandbox put on disk.
- The Ideas entry for several agents in one workspace has the tests as its first try.

##### docs: TODO.md is the todo list, its split completed

`TODO.md` still had the headings of the records that moved out of it, each over a pointer, and
its `validate-anchors` and `push --amend` entries had grown hard to read. The headings go and the
entries are reworked.

- `TODO.md` is what we might do and nothing else: its intro, `## Waiting`, `## Todo`, and
  `## Ideas`.
  - `## Continuation notes`, `## In Progress`, `## Closed`, and `## Bugs` are removed, and the
    intro names `zDOING.md`, `zCLOSED.md`, and `bugs.md` in their place.
  - The split is completed for the file and not for the agent-files, which still name
    `TODO.md` for all four. That is left to the entry for the record's move.
- The three `validate-anchors` entries are one, a bullet for each known issue.
  - A fourth issue is new: a code span that wraps onto a second line hides a citation after it.
    Two of the three failures of a whole-repo run are that, and both are false.
  - A heading in `TODO.md` lost its backticks, which stepped around the code-span slug fault
    and fixed nothing.
- The `push --amend` entry is grouped by side: what the work-repo commit keeps and takes, what
  the new agent-repo commit is, and the approval.
  - The title and body are optional, and the new trailer goes at the bottom of the list.

##### docs: the session lock closing

The trapezoid is created, wink's call for the close-out shape, and `vc-x1 validate` passed.

- This commit is the trapezoid's merge. Land gives it its two parents,
  `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md` first and the fourth rung second, and moves
  `main` forward onto it.

# References

[2]: #docs-the-session-lock-is-settled-as-flock
[3]: #docs-two-sessions-in-one-workspace-tested
[4]: #docs-the-session-lock-closing

11	## jj Basics
12	
13	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
14	rewrite, [why](rationale.md#jj-basics)). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be
15	driven with raw `git`, but this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid
16	trailers) is expressed in jj terms.
17	Reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There is no `jj mv`:
18	to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by content.
19	
20	Below, `<repo>` is either side's path and `<agent-dir>` the agent-repo's, which the work-repo's
21	`.vc-config.md` names under `[repos] agent` ([.vc-config.md](#vc-configmd)) rather than any
22	fixed directory.
23	
24	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R <agent-dir>`: show working copy status
25	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R <agent-dir>`: show commit log
26	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
27	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
28	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag: jj pushes new
29	  bookmarks without special flags)
30	- `jj bookmark set <name> -r <rev> -R <repo>`: create the bookmark, or move an existing one, at
31	  `<rev>`. Moving it backwards needs `--allow-backwards`
32	- `jj git push --named <name>=<rev> -R <repo>`: create *and* publish in one step, which is the usual
33	  way a cycle's bookmark is born (see [Cycle bookmarks](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land))
34	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it and
35	  creates a new empty working copy on top.
36	- The agent-repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
37	  updates continuously.
38	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
39	
40	Viewing, for a review: `jj diff -R .` is the working copy, `jj diff -r @- -R .` the previous commit,
41	`jj show -r <X> -R .` one revision's description and diff. Never `jj edit -r @-` to view a past
42	commit: it marks it mutable and shifts `@`.
43	
44	## Revsets
45	
46	How commits are addressed in `-r` arguments, condensed. jj's own semantics are the one dialect
47	([why](rationale.md#revsets)). The full language is `jj help -k revsets`, the single authority, and
48	the worked tutorial with terminal transcripts is `jj-tips.md`, hosted once in the template
49	repository.
50	
51	- A revision is `@` (the working copy), a chid prefix, or a commit id. Unambiguous prefixes are
52	  accepted, and ambiguous ones are rejected, never guessed.
53	- Neighbors: `@-` parent, `@--` grandparent, `@+` child. A step past the end of the chain is the
54	  empty set, not an error.
55	- `::` is the primary range operator, symmetric and endpoint-inclusive:
56	  - `::x` ancestors of x, including x. `x::` descendants of x, including x
57	  - `x::y` the DAG path: descendants of x that are also ancestors of y
58	- `..` is git-compatible set subtraction, not a tighter `::`:
59	  - `x..y` is `::y ~ ::x`: ancestors of y that are not ancestors of x
60	  - `x..` is `~::x`: every visible commit that is not an ancestor of x. Open-ended, so on a repo
61	    with parked branches it includes commits unrelated to x
62	  - `..x` is `::x ~ root()`: ancestors of x, excluding the root
63	- Useful sets: `jj log` (default revset), `jj log -r ::@` (all ancestors of `@`),
64	  `jj log -r 'all()'` (all visible commits), `jj evolog -r X` (one change's rewrite history),
65	  `jj op log` (operation history).
66	
67	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
68	
69	The cross-reference between the work-repo and the agent-repo is what makes the dual-repo work: every
70	commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the "why / how"
71	(session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID) git trailer
72	([why](rationale.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)).
73	
74	A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s (unlike
75	the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the counterpart
76	commit's chid behind a prefix naming the repo it lives in:
77	
78	- The prefix names a side, not a location. `/` refers to the work-repo and `/.claude` to the
79	  agent-repo, and each repo's own location is the path the work-repo's `.vc-config.md` declares,
80	  `[repos] work` and `[repos] agent`. The agent one may be any reachable relative path, under
81	  the work-repo's tree or outside it, and the `.claude` in the label is a constant that says
82	  nothing about it, so a sweep over the agent-repo's directory leaves every trailer alone.
83	- Which label a commit takes is decided by reading a repo's own `.vc-config.md`, its
84	  `[repos] agent` resolved relative to that file and compared against the directory holding it.
85	  So the config picks the side and the label is a constant, and the two never need to agree.
86	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work-repo**.
87	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **agent-repo**.
88	
89	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the chid's
90	**12-character** prefix:
91	
92	```
93	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to an agent-repo change
94	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
95	```
96	
97	How many, and which direction:
98	
99	- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<agent-chid>`, the agent-repo's change ID.
100	- **The agent-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push. The
101	  count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as they
102	  landed still carries exactly one. More than one occurs when a single push publishes several
103	  work-repo commits.
104	
105	Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,agent -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work-repo, second agent
106	repo).
107	
108	`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**. Never hand-write them into a commit body or
109	`--title`/`--body`.
110	
111	## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do
112	
113	`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
114	and body (`--yes` because push's gates need a tty the agent sandbox lacks, and the user's approval
115	of the shown title and body already covers them), stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer
116	([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent
117	repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in mind:
118	
119	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
120	  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
121	  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
122	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its work is
123	  already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work` but before
124	  the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` by hand is the rest of it.
125	- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** ([No hand-written
126	  trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
127	- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.**
128	  - One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
129	    bookmark the work-repo is on.
130	  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
131	    the wrong remote ref.
132	- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
133	  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
134	    the squash.
135	  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
136	  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
137	
138	A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
139	re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
140	
141	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
142	
143	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
144	coordinating with everyone involved first**
145	([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
146	and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
147	described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
148	covered. That is a [local
149	ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.
150	
151	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
152	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
153	stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
154	`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.
155	
156	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
157	
158	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
159	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
160	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
161	
162	**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
163	algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
164	and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
165	
166	- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
167	  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
168	- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
169	  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
170	  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
171	- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
172	  ready to be seen.
173	
174	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
175	`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
176	stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
177	closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
178	rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
179	
180	1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
181	   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
182	   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
183	   (`@` sits directly above it).
184	2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
185	   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
186	   as it is.
187	3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
188	   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
189	4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
190	   cycle anymore.
191	5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
192	   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
193	   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
194	   disposal once fully merged.
195	
196	- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
197	  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
198	- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
199	  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
200	
201	**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
202	bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):
203	
204	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
205	  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
206	  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
207	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
208	- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
209	  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
210	
211	## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
212	
213	A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
214	carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
215	holder.
216	
217	- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
218	- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
219	- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
220	  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
221	- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
222	  locally and remotely
223	
224	The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
225	freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
226	one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
227	rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.
228	
229	## Close-out shapes
230	
231	The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
232	[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
233	is one commit and lands as it is:
234	
235	- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
236	  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
237	  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
238	  by the landing fast-forward itself.
239	- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.
240	
241	Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
242	rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
243	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
244	
245	**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
246	whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
247	described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
248	trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
249	and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.

  creates a new empty working copy on top.

  updates continuously.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without

([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged

A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
holder.

- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
  locally and remotely

The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Close-out shapes

The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
is one commit and lands as it is:

- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
  by the landing fast-forward itself.
- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.

Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.
