# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

# Agent-files size

The line count of the agent-files, one row per landing that changed them, so the set's size is
tracked over time. A cycle that leaves the agent-files untouched adds no row, since a row saying
the count did not move records nothing. Smaller is the quasi-goal: a rule stated once is shorter
than a rule stated three times, and a shrinking count is evidence the set is converging, while a
growing one is a prompt to ask what arrived as a paragraph that should have been a line. The count
is not a rule, and a rule is never cut to move it.

A finding from the proposal cycle (2026-08-27), for whoever next tries a cut: a draft that cut
AGENTS.md from 370 to 320 lines with every rule kept found that the remaining bulk is the rules
themselves, so a further cut has to cut rules, and that is a convention decision, not an edit.

The count is `wc -l` over `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`, and `agent-data/*.md`, the total leaving out
`rationale.md`, taken at the close-out of a cycle that changed an agent-file and recorded here as
the closing rung's last edit, with the cycle title as the row's label. `rationale.md` is out of the
total because it is the rules' why and grows with every rule that gains one, so a rule gaining a
why does not read as the set growing. Rows before v0.2.5 counted it.

`vc-x1 agent-files size` takes the count and slides the per-file table, a new leftmost column in
and the oldest out. It is dry-run by default and `--no-dry-run` writes the file, `--label=TEXT`
names a column the set's version file cannot, and the `## Counts` row above stays a hand's work,
since its note is prose.

| 2026-09-04 | agent-files(adoption): v0.2.0 | 10 | 2231 | iiac-perf's set verbatim: `## Closed` last in the Todo format list, `# References` named, the re-pack parenthetical dropped |

### docs: the session lock is turned off

(wink, 2026-10-13) The session lock, `.agent-running`, is an instruction in `custom.md` that every
session follows at acquaint: a probe, a background holder, and a sentence. It guards against two
sessions in one workspace, which one user with one session at a time does not have, so the cost
is paid at every acquaint for a case that does not come up. No Todo entry was picked. The entry
nearest it, the proposal of the lock to the set with the instruction's two faults, is ended by
this cycle.

#### Deliberation

- The lock is turned off and not deleted, wink's call.
  - The instruction is kept word for word in [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), and
    `custom.md` keeps an entry that says the lock is off and where the instruction is, so turning
    it on is moving the text back.
  - The entry says off in its first words. Acquaint has a session do what `custom.md` asks, and
    a bare pointer at an instruction could be read as the instruction.
  - `.gitignore` keeps its `/.agent-running` line, so a lock turned on again needs no second edit,
    and the file a session left on disk stays ignored.
- The cost accepted: nothing keeps a second session out of the workspace.
  - Two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, a title that does not say what its commit
    holds and a trailer that names the wrong session, as the tests of 2026-10-12 showed.
  - One session per workspace is then the user's habit and no longer a check.
- The proposal of the lock to the set is dropped, and what it had worked out is kept beside the
  instruction: `flock` being a Linux tool, the thought of a small `vc-x1` command in its place,
  and the instruction's two faults.
  - The faults no longer bite, there being no instruction to forget or to edit.
- The session that makes this cycle keeps the holder it took at its acquaint.
  - The edit reaches the sessions started after it, which is one of the two faults, and here it
    is what is wanted: stopping the holder by hand shows that an agent did as it was told and
    nothing about the instruction.
- The Todo entry for the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run still says the session lock keeps a second
  agent out. It is left as it is, wink's call, since the next cycle removes the entry.
- A single-step cycle, with a bare version and no `-dev` name, the cycle being documents alone.

#### Solution

The instruction moves out of `custom.md` into [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), and
`custom.md` says the lock is off and points there.

- The notes file says the lock is off, holds the instruction as it was, and says what turning it
  on again would want settled.
- The Todo entry for the proposal to the set is removed. The scratch its tests left is an entry
  of its own, wink's to delete.
- The Ideas entry for several agents in one workspace no longer says the lock refuses them.

#### Acceptance check

- `vc-x1 validate` passes.
- `grep -c flock custom.md` prints 0.
- A session started after Land acquaints without running `flock` and without saying "Lock
  taken.", and `flock -xn .agent-running true` run from another terminal while that session works
  exits 0.

#### Ladder

- docs: the session lock is turned off (current)

[package]
name = "vc-x1"
version = "0.84.27"
edition = "2024"

# Single-name convention (chores-16, 0.78.3): the package name IS
# the installed binary's name, `vc-x1` on main and a per-line dev
# name on a branch (renamed at cycle open, back at close-out, next
# to the version bump). The guard against a forgotten open-rename
# is build.rs, which refuses to build a suffixed version under the
# stable name on every cargo verb, `cargo install` included.

[lints.clippy]
# The process-spawn ban: `Command::new` is disallowed via
# clippy.toml's `disallowed-methods`, and deny (not warn) so a bare
# new spawn site fails `cargo clippy` even without `-D warnings`.
# The documented allowlist lives in clippy.toml.
disallowed_methods = "deny"

[dependencies]
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["now"] }
clap = { version = "4.6", features = ["derive", "wrap_help"] }
clap_complete = { version = "4.6", features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }
futures = "0.3"
# The gix jj-lib 0.45 resolves (no features of our own): the
# session's lock-contention downcast needs type identity with the
# errors jj-lib returns, and init's bare-repo creation reuses it.
gix = { version = "0.87", default-features = false }
# When raising jj-lib: check whether it now offers the commits a
# remote's bookmarks are on without fetching. If so, `git_command`
# in src/jj/session.rs and its two callers take it, and
# clippy.toml's register entry 6 closes (TODO.md > ## Waiting).
jj-lib = "0.45"
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std"] }
pollster = "1.0"
serde_json = "1"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]
libc = "0.2"

cat >> notes/session-lock.md <<'EOF'

## Turned off

The lock is off since 2026-10-13, wink's call: what it costs is more than what it prevents here.

- The cost was paid by every session: a probe and a background command at each acquaint, a
  sentence to say, and a holder to keep alive for as long as the session ran.
- What it prevented is two sessions in one workspace, and this workspace has one user who runs one
  session at a time.
- The instruction had two faults, below, and each could stop a session that was alone.
- What is given up: nothing keeps a second session out. Two sessions lose no data and leave a
  wrong record, as [What two sessions do with no lock](#what-two-sessions-do-with-no-lock) found,
  and one session per workspace is the user's to keep.
- What stays: this file, and the `/.agent-running` line in `.gitignore`.

## The instruction, as it was

The entry in `custom.md > ## Project conventions and overrides`, first in its list, word for word
as it stood from 2026-10-11 until it was taken out:

```
- Lock: at acquaint, before anything else, a session runs `flock -xn .agent-running true` at the
  workspace root, alone. If it fails, the session responds with the one sentence "Another session
  holds `.agent-running`, stopping." and runs no further command, not even to find the holder. If
  it succeeds, the session starts `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background
  command, leaves it running, and says "Lock taken." If that command exits while the session
  runs, the same sentence and the same stop. A session that already holds one does neither. A
  resumed session is told its holder was stopped with the earlier process, and it runs both
  again before anything else, as at acquaint. This keeps a second session from working in the
  workspace, so two cannot push or amend at once.
```

## Turning it on again

Turning the lock on is putting the entry above back into `custom.md`, in place of the entry that
says the lock is off. What was known and left unsettled when it was turned off:

- The instruction has two faults, and neither had a fix planned:
  - A session that has forgotten it holds the lock probes again at a reacquaint, fails against
    its own holder, and stops as if another session held it.
  - An edit to the instruction reaches only the sessions started after it.
- The lock was to be proposed to the set, and was not. `flock` is a Linux tool and the instruction
  was this project's, and both wanted an answer first.
  - macOS has the `flock` call and does not ship the tool, and Windows has neither.
  - We think the answer is a small `vc-x1` command that takes the lock and holds it, through
    Rust's `File::try_lock`: `flock` on Linux and macOS, `LockFileEx` on Windows, and each system
    drops the lock when the holder dies.
  - That is code in `vc-x1` for the session lock, which the decision of 2026-10-12 was against.
    It weighed races and not other systems.
- The hook that takes the lock in the agent's place is designed and not built ([What a hook
  could do](#what-a-hook-could-do)).
EOF

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
no hook is built.

## What the lock is today

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. It is
off since 2026-10-13 ([Turned off](#turned-off)), and the instruction is kept here ([The
instruction, as it was](#the-instruction-as-it-was)). This file also holds what was found out
about the lock on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's place, and what
happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's own tests, of
2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, no hook is built, and the
instruction, kept on 2026-10-12, was taken out of `custom.md` the day after.

## What the lock is when it is on

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

## What was decided

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
  above.
- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
  sandbox's names into
  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.

# Notes

This directory contains various notes and documentation related to the project. Each file is
organized by topic for easy reference.

The chores-NN.md files in [chores/](chores) and [done.md](done.md) are frozen history: the records
of cycles that closed before the cycle-record rule ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
Nothing is appended to them. They stay until the agent-repo transcripts are comfortable to read a
cycle from, then both retire in one cycle after a permalink sweep of the links into them (the `##
Waiting` entry in [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)). A cycle's live record is [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)'s `##
In Progress` block, and a closed cycle's is its `## Closed` block in the landmark commit's tree.

On trial since the cycle "feat: sync is safe by default" (2026-10-09), a cycle's record is kept in
[../zDOING.md](../zDOING.md) instead, the agent-files not yet saying so, and that cycle's landmark
holds its finished block there.

Tool architecture lives at the repo root in [`../ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md): the
CLI-args / `Context`+`Params` split, a generic module map, the subcommand model, and what the
Context+Params port and the options_flags extraction *are* (the *live status* is in the chores
files).

Multi-cycle programs too big for a TODO.md entry get their own dated plan file, e.g.
[refactor-20260716.md](refactor-20260716.md) (typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process): one `##`
section per stage, so chores and todo entries can reference a stage by anchor. The plan file owns
the forward design; chores still records each shipped cycle.

A rule that governs what the tool does, rather than a record of what was done, gets its own topic
file so it can be found without knowing which cycle produced it, e.g.
[jj-version-policy.md](jj-version-policy.md). The investigation behind such a rule stays where it
happened (a plan file or a chores section) and is linked from the policy, so neither restates the
other.

The agent-files' line count over time is in [agent-files-size.md](agent-files-size.md), one row
per landing, smaller being the quasi-goal. `vc-x1 agent-files size` takes the count and slides
that file's per-file window.

The session lock, `.agent-running`, and what two agent sessions in one workspace do without it,
are in [session-lock.md](session-lock.md): what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's place,
three tests of two sessions with no lock, and what was decided.

How a change to a line in any work-repo file is connected to its discussion in the agent-repo,
the partner commit, its time-window, and the transcript write, is in
[transcript-write.md](transcript-write.md). It carries the objective and the terms, the by-hand
procedure, the two decisions the probes settled, the `vc-x1 lookup` command's requirements in
their one home, what building the command found, and the probes themselves, three cycles of them.
`vc-x1 lookup` does the procedure in both directions, and the fixture it is tested over is built
by `support/fixtures/build-dr-1.py`.

In the future I expect we may want to create a "notes" database to better manage the information,
TBD.

General maintenance tasks and considerations for the project see other files for
more specific topics. A chore in a chores file provides quick information on the
how and why of a particular chore.

# Notes

This directory contains various notes and documentation related to the project. Each file is
organized by topic for easy reference.

The chores-NN.md files in [chores/](chores) and [done.md](done.md) are frozen history: the records
of cycles that closed before the cycle-record rule ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
Nothing is appended to them. They stay until the agent-repo transcripts are comfortable to read a
cycle from, then both retire in one cycle after a permalink sweep of the links into them (the `##
Waiting` entry in [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)). A cycle's live record is [../TODO.md](../TODO.md)'s `##
In Progress` block, and a closed cycle's is its `## Closed` block in the landmark commit's tree.

On trial since the cycle "feat: sync is safe by default" (2026-10-09), a cycle's record is kept in
[../zDOING.md](../zDOING.md) instead, the agent-files not yet saying so, and that cycle's landmark
holds its finished block there.

Tool architecture lives at the repo root in [`../ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md): the
CLI-args / `Context`+`Params` split, a generic module map, the subcommand model, and what the
Context+Params port and the options_flags extraction *are* (the *live status* is in the chores
files).

Multi-cycle programs too big for a TODO.md entry get their own dated plan file, e.g.
[refactor-20260716.md](refactor-20260716.md) (typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process): one `##`
section per stage, so chores and todo entries can reference a stage by anchor. The plan file owns
the forward design, and chores still records each shipped cycle.

A rule that governs what the tool does, rather than a record of what was done, gets its own topic
file so it can be found without knowing which cycle produced it, e.g.
[jj-version-policy.md](jj-version-policy.md). The investigation behind such a rule stays where it
happened (a plan file or a chores section) and is linked from the policy, so neither restates the
other.

The agent-files' line count over time is in [agent-files-size.md](agent-files-size.md), one row
per landing, smaller being the quasi-goal. `vc-x1 agent-files size` takes the count and slides
that file's per-file window.

The session lock, `.agent-running`, and what two agent sessions in one workspace do without it,
are in [session-lock.md](session-lock.md): what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's place,
three tests of two sessions with no lock, and what was decided.

How a change to a line in any work-repo file is connected to its discussion in the agent-repo,
the partner commit, its time-window, and the transcript write, is in
[transcript-write.md](transcript-write.md). It carries the objective and the terms, the by-hand
procedure, the two decisions the probes settled, the `vc-x1 lookup` command's requirements in
their one home, what building the command found, and the probes themselves, three cycles of them.
`vc-x1 lookup` does the procedure in both directions, and the fixture it is tested over is built
by `support/fixtures/build-dr-1.py`.

TBD.

Usage: vc-x1 agent-files size [OPTIONS] [DIR]

Arguments:
  [DIR]
          A directory holding a copy of the set [default: this workspace]

Options:
      --file <PATH>
          The notes file whose per-file table slides [default:
          DIR/notes/agent-files-size.md]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --label <TEXT>
          The new column's label, `--label=TEXT` when it opens on a `-`
          [default: the set's version file]

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --no-dry-run
          Slide the table in place [default: dry-run]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

## In Progress

### docs: turn off the session lock

(wink, 2026-10-13) The session lock, `.agent-running`, is an instruction in `custom.md` that every
session follows at acquaint: a probe, a background holder, and a sentence. It guards against two
sessions in one workspace, which one user with one session at a time does not have, so the cost
is paid at every acquaint for a case that does not come up. No Todo entry was picked. The entry
nearest it, the proposal of the lock to the set with the instruction's two faults, is ended by
this cycle.

#### Deliberation

- The lock is turned off and not deleted, wink's call.
  - The instruction is kept word for word in [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), and
    `custom.md` keeps an entry that says the lock is off and where the instruction is, so turning
    it on is moving the text back.
  - The entry says off in its first words. Acquaint has a session do what `custom.md` asks, and
    a bare pointer at an instruction could be read as the instruction.
  - `.gitignore` keeps its `/.agent-running` line, so a lock turned on again needs no second edit,
    and the file a session left on disk stays ignored.
- The cost accepted: nothing keeps a second session out of the workspace.
  - Two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, a title that does not say what its commit
    holds and a trailer that names the wrong session, as the tests of 2026-10-12 showed.
  - One session per workspace is then the user's habit and no longer a check.
- The proposal of the lock to the set is dropped, and what it had worked out is kept beside the
  instruction: `flock` being a Linux tool, the thought of a small `vc-x1` command in its place,
  and the instruction's two faults.
  - The faults no longer bite, there being no instruction to forget or to edit.
- The session that makes this cycle keeps the holder it took at its acquaint.
  - The edit reaches the sessions started after it, which is one of the two faults, and here it
    is what is wanted: stopping the holder by hand shows that an agent did as it was told and
    nothing about the instruction.
- The Todo entry for the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run still says the session lock keeps a second
  agent out. It is left as it is, the agent's placing, since the next cycle removes the entry.
- A single-step cycle, with a bare version and no `-dev` name, the cycle being documents alone.

#### Solution

The instruction moves out of `custom.md` into [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), and
`custom.md` says the lock is off and points there.

- The notes file says the lock is off, holds the instruction as it was, and says what turning it
  on again would want settled.
- The Todo entry for the proposal to the set is removed. The scratch its tests left is an entry
  of its own, wink's to delete.
- The Ideas entry for several agents in one workspace no longer says the lock refuses them.

#### Acceptance check

- `vc-x1 validate` passes.
- `grep -c flock custom.md` prints 0.
- A session started after Land acquaints without running `flock` and without saying "Lock
  taken.", and `flock -xn .agent-running true` run from another terminal while that session works
  exits 0.

#### Ladder

- docs: the session lock is turned off (current)

# References
